proposed_edges.evidence_note: Existing readings. Telling the Truth about History (appleby_hunt_jacob): all three authors share every chapter; the chapter 7 "Practical Realism" section and notes name Putnam and Peirce as resources; chapter 8: "It is time to come out of the trenches." Beyond the Cultural Turn (bonnell_hunt_primary): the editors' introduction (pp. 1, 12–25 read) presents competing reassessments and explicitly acknowledges White's disagreement in his afterword. proposed_edges.relationship: Globalization as the paradigm succeeding Marxism, modernization, Annales and identity politics, questioned for privileging economics and for threatening the gains of cultural history, as her reviewer summarises Writing History in the Global Era (2014)
proposed_edges.map_label: Writing History in the Global Era, 2014 (per McClure)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Reviewer evidence only; the book is unread here. Julia McClure (Reviews in History 1732, 2015; read via WebFetch extraction, and in full by the second research pass) summarises the argument: globalization has become a dominant "paradigm" replacing Marxism, modernization, the Annales school and identity politics; it privileges economics and macro trends and risks overshadowing "society" and "self"; and it "potentially threatens to wash away the gains of the last decades of cultural history" (Hunt, p. 59, as McClure quotes her). McClure criticises Hunt for not naming proponents of the paradigm and for treating world or global history as the history of globalization. This atlas was first developed around the book; its own words should replace this reviewer summary when read. Further pages as McClure quotes them: globalization "asserts the inescapability of the process, the primacy of economics in driving it" (p. 55); "historians need to contest the terrain it now claims, using the tools held out by cultural theories" (p. 43). McClure: her criticism "is not a criticism of historical genre, but of ideology".

proposed_edges.relationship: Human rights made “self-evident” through imagined empathy, epistolary novels and the rejection of torture, 1760s–1790s, as reviewers summarise Inventing Human Rights (2007)
proposed_edges.evidence_note: Reviewer evidence only; the book is unread here. David A. Bell (LRB, 15 November 2007; read via WebFetch extraction) summarises it: epistolary novels such as Pamela, Clarissa and Julie taught readers to identify with others; torture was condemned by the 1780s; a "logic of rights" followed the 1789 Declaration; he calls the method "the new cultural history", which Hunt had popularised, and finds the 2007 book keeping the thesis of The Family Romance of the French Revolution (1992). Samuel Moyn (The Nation, 16 April 2007) reports her dating of the cause to "the Enlightenment and the age of democratic revolutions" and "the cascading logic of human rights". Their criticisms are drawn on the critique arrow from intellectual history. A second contribution to cultural history, distinct from the 1989 introduction (edge_756).

proposed_edges.relationship: Inventing Human Rights criticised for reading late-twentieth-century human rights back into the eighteenth century and for making “rights themselves” its protagonists (Moyn, 2007), and for a cultural-history method that flattens texts and actions (Bell, 2007)
proposed_edges.map_label: Moyn and Bell on Inventing Human Rights, 2007
proposed_edges.evidence_note: This arrow represents Samuel Moyn's and David A. Bell's specified criticisms, not a verdict of intellectual history. Moyn (The Nation, 16 April 2007; complete text read via WebFetch extraction): the new human-rights history "distorts the past to suit the present"; "rights talk" had "historical lineages completely different from humanitarianism"; "The protagonists of her book are not people thinking and acting on their convictions but rights themselves"; there is "little reason to locate the 'invention' of human rights as we now know them in the late eighteenth century", since they are "an invention of recent date". Bell (LRB 29:22, 15 November 2007; complete text read via WebFetch extraction): the account after 1789 through the present is compressed into 38 pages, concentrating on 1948, novels crowd out theatre and painting, ordinary people who read no novels also embraced rights, and the new cultural history tends to flatten the difference between texts and actions; he still calls the book "a rich, elegant and persuasive essay". Moyn's later book-length argument (The Last Utopia, 2010) is unread here.

verification.note: Complete text read via WebFetch extraction for revision 1.144 (no pagination). Bell's summary: epistolary novels (Pamela, Clarissa, Julie) taught identification with others; torture condemned by the 1780s; a "logic of rights" after 1789. Criticisms: the account after 1789 through the present is compressed into 38 pages, concentrating on 1948 (the second research pass quotes "the period after 1789 'in a breezy 38 pages'"); he reports Moyn's criticism and calls it "partly misplaced"; novels at the expense of theatre, painting and emulation; causation hinted at; ordinary people who did not read novels also embraced rights; the "new cultural history" tends to flatten texts and actions. He calls her French Revolution studies "luminous", reads The Family Romance (1992) as tracing family imagery from paternal monarchy to fraternal republic, a thesis the 2007 book keeps, and credits her with popularising "the new cultural history". Verdict: "a rich, elegant and persuasive essay" that "raises more questions than it can answer".

hunt.note: Revision 1.144: the stored PDF URL now returns HTML; the review was read via WebFetch extraction at https://reviews.history.ac.uk/review/1732/print. Julia McClure, review of Lynn Hunt, Writing History in the Global Era (Norton, 2014), Reviews in History no. 1732 (19 February 2015). Her summary: globalization has become a dominant "paradigm" filling the place of Marxism, modernization, the Annales school and identity politics, privileging economics and macro trends and threatening to overshadow "society" and "self"; Hunt surveys the cultural theories (Foucault, Derrida) she helped bring into history, defending their gains and acknowledging their limits; Hunt is quoted as saying globalization "potentially threatens to wash away the gains of the last decades of cultural history" (p. 59, as McClure cites it). McClure's criticisms: no proponents of the paradigm named; global history equated with the history of globalization; Hunt's own standpoint on universal values needs the scrutiny she applies to Mignolo. The book itself is unread. The second research pass (evidence-hunt.pass2.md §6) read the review in full (4-page PDF) and records Hunt's words with the book's pages as McClure gives them: globalization "asserts the inescapability of the process, the primacy of economics in driving it" (p. 55); "the globalization paradigm reinstates the very suppositions that cultural theories had criticized, and thus potentially threatens to wash away the gains of the last decades of cultural history" (p. 59); "historians need to contest the terrain it now claims, using the tools held out by cultural theories while remaining mindful of their limitations" (p. 43); "is it a Trojan horse that threatens to bring back old paradigms rather than offering a truly new one?" (p. 52). McClure: "Hunt's criticism of the globalization paradigm is not a criticism of historical genre, but of ideology."
